content: Epidural analgesia during labor is associated with a prolonged second stage of labor and an increased likelihood of instrumental delivery. It has been hypothesized that adopting a more upright maternal position during the second stage of labor might mitigate these adverse effects. This review aimed to evaluate the impact of different maternal birthing positions—upright versus recumbent—on maternal and fetal outcomes in women receiving epidural analgesia. The review included eight randomized controlled trials involving 4,464 women. These trials compared upright positions with recumbent positions during the second stage of labor. Five of the studies were conducted in the UK, one in France, and two in Spain. The largest UK trial contributed the majority of participants and was assessed as having a low risk of bias. However, other studies varied in their quality, with some showing unclear or high risks of bias due to issues such as selection bias, attrition bias, or co-interventions. The evidence suggests that there may be little or no difference between upright and recumbent positions in terms of the combined primary outcome of operative birth (defined as either cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery). The average risk ratio (RR) for operative birth was 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70 to 1.07), based on low-quality evidence. Similarly, the impact of upright positions on cesarean section rates (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.46) and instrumental vaginal births (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.12) remains uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. The duration of the second stage of labor also showed no clear difference between positions (mean difference [MD] 6.00 minutes, 95% CI −37.46 to 49.46), but the evidence was again of very low quality. Regarding postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), there was probably little or no difference between the two positions in terms of PPH requiring blood transfusion (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.72; moderate-quality evidence). Maternal satisfaction with the overall childbirth experience was slightly lower in the upright group (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.92 to 0.99). However, fewer babies in the upright group were born with low cord pH, which is a marker of fetal acidosis (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.90; moderate-quality evidence). Other maternal and fetal outcomes, such as birth canal trauma requiring suturing (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.13; low-quality evidence), abnormal fetal heart patterns requiring intervention (RR 1.69, 95% CI 0.32 to 8.84; very low-quality evidence), and neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.02 to 12.73; very low-quality evidence), showed no clear differences between the two positions. However, the confidence intervals for these outcomes were wide, leaving the possibility of clinically significant effects. A sensitivity analysis of studies with a low risk of bias revealed that upright positions might increase the likelihood of operative birth (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.20; high-quality evidence). This increase was primarily driven by a higher rate of cesarean sections in the upright group (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.57; high-quality evidence), equating to 25 additional cesarean sections per 1,000 women. There was no clear impact on instrumental vaginal births in this analysis (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.30; low-quality evidence). In conclusion, there may be little or no difference in the overall rate of operative births between upright and recumbent positions during the second stage of labor for women with epidural analgesia. However, the evidence is limited by heterogeneity among studies, differences in study design, and potential biases. Sensitivity analyses suggest that recumbent positions may reduce the need for operative births, particularly cesarean sections, without increasing the rate of instrumental deliveries. Women may also report greater satisfaction with their childbirth experience when adopting a recumbent position. It is important to note that the recumbent positions studied in this review included left or right lateral and semi-recumbent positions, rather than flat supine or lithotomy positions, which are generally avoided due to the risk of aorto-caval compression.
